topic: The Pi Collision Mystery: Why Colliding Blocks Compute Pi
target_audience: Undergraduate Physics/Math students and advanced High School students

sections.title: The Impossible Experiment
sections.content: Introduce a frictionless environment with a wall, a small block (Mass m = 1kg), and a much larger block (Mass M = 100^N kg). When the large block is pushed toward the small one, they collide multiple times (including wall bounces). The total number of collisions surprisingly yields the digits of Pi.
sections.example: Imagine a curious Penguin watching a 1kg ice cube and a massive 10,000kg iceberg colliding. If the iceberg moves at the ice cube, they will collide exactly 314 times before moving away.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Laws of the Game
sections.content: Establish the two fundamental rules: Conservation of Momentum and Conservation of Energy. Explain that since collisions are perfectly elastic, no energy is lost as heat. Introduce the 'Velocity State Space' where we plot the velocity of block 1 (v1) on the x-axis and block 2 (v2) on the y-axis.
sections.example: Visualize a 2D graph where a single dot represents the 'speed state' of both blocks simultaneously. As they hit each other, the dot jumps to a new position on this map.

sections.title: The Energy Ellipse to Energy Circle
sections.content: Show the Energy equation: (1/2)mv1² + (1/2)Mv2² = Total Energy. In standard coordinates, this is an ellipse. To simplify, we rescale the x-axis by multiplying v1 by √m and the y-axis by √M. This transformation turns the ellipse into a perfect circle.
sections.example: An animation shows the 'squashed' ellipse stretching vertically until it becomes a perfect circle, centered at the origin, representing all possible velocity combinations for a fixed energy.

sections.title: Collisions as Geometric Reflections
sections.content: Explain that every collision (block-to-block or block-to-wall) corresponds to a reflection in this state space. A wall collision is a simple vertical reflection. A block collision is a reflection across a specific line determined by the mass ratio. Each collision 'jumps' an arc length along the circle.
sections.example: Imagine a beam of light (the state dot) bouncing inside a circular mirror. Each 'clack' sound we hear in the real world is a 'flash' of light hitting the circle's edge.

sections.title: The Pi Connection: Arc Length and Wrapping
sections.content: As the large block pushes the small one, the state dot moves around the circle in equal angular steps. The size of the angle depends on the mass ratio. As the mass ratio becomes 100^N, the angle becomes infinitesimally small. The number of steps to traverse the circle is essentially the circumference (containing Pi) divided by the step size.
sections.example: Using a mass ratio of 100:1, we see the 'light beam' take many small steps. If we count them, we get 31 collisions. At 10,000:1, we get 314. The math reveals that we are literally 'measuring' the perimeter of a circle using collisions.

sections.title: Summary: The Geometry of Physics
sections.content: Conclude by highlighting how a physical problem (blocks hitting each other) is hidden geometry in disguise. Reiterate that Pi is not just about circles, but a fundamental property of how energy and momentum relate through squares.
sections.example: A final visual montage: The Penguin watches the blocks stop colliding just as the 'state dot' completes its journey around the circle, with the counter displaying the digits of Pi: 3.14159...
